title: Weld current and penetration depth
intro:
A welding engineer made ten test welds at currents from 120 to 210 A and sectioned each to measure the penetration depth (mm). Take x = current and y = depth.

Find the least-squares intercept b₀ and slope b₁, and use the line to predict the depth at 175 A. b₀ can come out negative: 0 A is far outside the data, so it is only a fitting constant (item 11.2). Give b₀ and the predicted depth to two decimals, and b₁ to four decimals (it is small: about how many mm one more ampere adds).

To use the Workbench: press **Copy the data**, press Ctrl+B, click **+ Data table** and paste (Ctrl+V). Choose **Simple linear regression** in the list on the left, set **x column** to *Current (A)*, **y column** to *Depth (mm)* and **Predict at x₀, optional** to 175. Read **Intercept (b₀)**, **Slope (b₁)** and **Fitted y at x₀**. Ctrl+L brings you back.

Slope.says: That is the slope of x on y (S_xy / S_yy): the current per mm of depth. Regress y on x: b₁ = S_xy / S_xx.

Intercept.says: Check the sign in b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄: subtract b₁x̄ from ȳ, do not add it.

hints: x̄ = 165 A. Work out ȳ, then S_xx = Σ(x − x̄)² and S_xy = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ).
b₁ = S_xy / S_xx, then b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄. The line goes through the point (x̄, ȳ).
The prediction is ŷ = b₀ + b₁ × 175. Keep b₁ to at least four decimals until the end: it is multiplied by 175.
